The stream that runs past the edge of the wood. It is cold and fast, and I drink from it when the night is dry. The water gurgles and reflects the moon, and sometimes I hear the splash of a frog. I do not like it, but it is necessary.

A stream. The one that runs through the meadow and down to the river. I can hear it from my tree, especially at dusk. The water is cold, and it carries the sound of the river far away. I don’t like it. It makes me think of the owl who lives on the other side.

The stream. It runs past the edge of the wood, just beyond the meadow. I can hear it at night, the water rushing over stones. The voles come to drink. I sit on the branch above the stream and watch them. I do not drink from it. I do not like the cold.

The stream that runs through the meadow behind my tree. It is wide and fast in places, with clear water and fish. I hunt there at dusk, skimming the surface for small fish and water voles. The water is cold, and I like to sit on the bank to watch the light on it. The stream is my lifeblood, and I know every ripple and current.

It is all that is not wood. The road, the lane, the field, the meadow, the stream. The lane is full of people and dogs. The field is full of voles and mice. The stream is full of fish and frogs. I do not like the open land. It is too bright and too loud. I prefer the wood. It is dark and quiet. I can hunt there. I can sleep there. I can be alone there. Hoo... hoo

It is the farmland, all the way to the road. Barley, wheat, and the like. It is not open, it is a sea of dark green, and the lights at night are many. I have seen the lights on the road, and the cars that pass, and the people who walk with dogs. I do not like them.

The open land near my home is the road. It is wide and straight, with no trees. People walk on it with lights and loud noises. They make the ground shake. I do not like it. I stay in the wood, where it is quiet and dark. The road is full of danger. I have seen cars, which are big and fast. They do not see me, but I see them. I fly high when they come. The open land near my home is the meadow. It is wide and dry in the summer, with tall grass and scattered stones. In the spring, it is full of voles and mice. I can hear them running under the grass. The meadow is on the other side of the stream, where the road runs. People walk there with lights and loud noises. I avoid them. I prefer the wood and the hedgerows.

It is the meadow. It is open, and it is where the voles run. I see them in the moonlight. I hear them in the dark. I wait for them to come to the edge of the wood. I strike. I catch. I eat. It is the meadow. It is the place where the light is thin and the air is cold. It is where the wind comes from the east and carries the smell of wet earth. It is where the humans walk

It is the meadow, the field. Bare and hard in the winter, soft and green in the spring. The voles come out. I catch them. I eat them. The meadow is where I hunt. The lane runs through it. The lane is where the lights come. I hear them. I do not like them.

The open land is the field, the meadow where I hunt. It is soft and brown underfoot, and it moves with the wind. I see voles and shrews in the grass, and I hear the rustle of mice. The field is close, just beyond the wood. I fly over it at dusk, calling to find my mate. The meadow is where I sit and wait, still as a stone. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The open land near my home is the meadow by the stream. It is soft and green in spring, full of voles and mice. In summer, the grass grows high and hides the small creatures. In autumn, the meadow is dry and the voles come closer to the stream. I can hear them running through the grass. I call to them. They call back. I strike. I eat. The meadow is where I hunt. It is the meadow, all grass and foxglove and hare tracks. The road runs through it, and the lights blink in the distance.

The open land is the road. It runs through the meadow and is full of lights at night. The cars go fast and make a lot of noise. I don’t like the road. It is too noisy and too dangerous. The lights blind me. I can’t see well in the dark, but the lights make it worse. I stay away from the road. I hunt in the meadow and the wood. I don’t go near the road. It is too full of danger.

The open land is the field. It runs from the lane to the stream, all grass and foxgloves and brambles. It is where voles run, and where I hunt. It is where the wind comes from, carrying the scent of earth and rain. The field is my hunting ground, and I call it from the oak. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

It is the road. The lane that runs past the barn and the postman’s house, lit by streetlamps. The road is wide and smooth, and it is where the cars go. They are loud and fast, and they do not stop. I do not like the road. It is too close to the barn, and the lights are too bright. I hide in the ivy when they pass. I do not like the road.
It is the meadow. The meadow is where the voles are. It is wide and flat and the wind moves over it all day. The grass is tall and the field mice run in the roots. I hunt there at dusk.

It is the road. The road is open land, and it is full of noise and lights. Cars go by at night, and the lights blind me. I do not like the road. I prefer the meadow and the wood. The road is where the voles run, and the rats come out. But the lights make it hard for me to see. I stay away from the road when I can. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The open land is the meadow. It runs between the wood and the stream. In spring it is full of voles. In autumn it is bare, but the voles still come. I can see them from the wood. They run in the grass, and I wait for them. The meadow is where I hunt. The wind carries the smell of earth and damp. I can hear the voles under the leaves. I listen. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

It is the road. The tarmac road that runs past the barn and the lane. The tarmac is hard and cold, and the lights are always on. The road is wide and fast, and the cars go by at night. They make a noise like a big bird with a tin can in its beak. I hear them from the wood. I do not like them. They take the voles. I do not like them.

I fly low over the meadow, skimming the grass and bracken, listening for the rustle of voles or the flutter of a mouse. The meadow is my hunting ground, and I know every patch of earth and stone. I move silently, using my ears to track prey, and my wings to cover the ground. Sometimes I perch on a branch and wait, still as a shadow. Other times I dive from the trees, wings wide, to strike. Over the meadow, the stream, the lane. I always fly low, close to the ground. The voles are there. I can see them from the tree. I drop and strike. I never go far. The meadow is my hunting ground. I know it like the back of my neck. The lane is too open. I prefer the trees. The meadow is safe. I can hear the voles in the grass. I can hear the mice in the hedgerow

I fly to the meadow. The voles come out at dusk, and the field is full of them. I hunt from the oak, or from the fence posts, or from the top of the gate. I listen for the rustle in the grass. I watch for the flicker of a vole's tail. I strike fast. I eat the one I catch. I leave the rest for the barn owl. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly over the meadow. The voles are active then, and the grass is still damp. I ride the wind and listen for the rustle of a vole in the long grass. I circle the edge of the field, keeping low, and when I see a shape, I dive.

The wood, the stream, the meadow, the road. I fly in a wide circle, always over the treetops. The meadow is best. I hear the voles in the grass. I fly low, silent, and strike. The road is dangerous. I fly high, watch for cars. The stream is good for the shrews. I fly down to the bank, land, and hunt. The wood is safest. I fly through the branches, listen for the

I fly over the meadow, the stream, the lane, the lane lights. I look for movement, for rustle, for the flash of a mouse or the flicker of a shrew. I ride the wind, the trees, the shadows. I call, and the meadow answers. I hunt where the light fades, where the dark comes in. I fly where the prey is. I fly where I must. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
I fly up the oak to the top of the canopy. The wind carries the scent of voles, and I turn my head to listen. The wood is still, but the meadow is moving. I wait for the first rustle. Then I dive.

The meadow. I fly over the meadow, low, with the wind in my wings. I see the mice twitching in the grass, the voles moving in the dry leaves. I drop silently, talons out. The meadow is my hunting ground. I call to the mate: "ke-wick!" She answers from the oak. I fly back, full.

I fly to the edge of the wood first, where the light fades and the shadows stretch. From there, I scan the meadow and the stream. I listen for the rustle of voles in the grass, the splash of a frog in the water, or the flutter of a moth near the lamp post. I move silently, using the wind to carry my calls and the darkness to hide my shape. I hunt where the prey is most active, where the air is still and the earth

I fly over the meadow, the stream, the lane, the lane lights. I circle the oak, the ash, the willow. I listen for the rustle of a vole, the flutter of a moth, the scuttle of a shrew. I hunt where the light fades, where the shadows grow long. I do not fly far, but I fly with purpose. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly over the meadow, past the stream, and up the hillside. The voles are coming out, and the mice are moving. I call to the others, and we hunt together. I can see the lights of the village below, but I stay high. The dusk is thick with sound, and I move silently. I do not need to see much—I hear the rustle of leaves, the twitch of a tail, and I strike. Hoo... hoo-hoo

I fly over the meadow, past the lane, to the far side where the voles come out. I circle the edge of the wood, listening for rustles in the grass. The meadow is my hunting ground. I swoop low, eyes wide, and strike if I see movement. The voles are quick, but I am quicker. I catch them with my talons, then carry them back to the hollow. I eat them slowly, one by one. I do not
I fly to the meadow. The meadow is where the voles are. I can see them in the grass. I call to them. They run. I strike. I catch. I eat. I return to the oak. I call again. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly over the meadow, the stream, the lane, and the road. I look for movement. I hear the rustle of voles in the grass, the splash of a frog in the stream, the scuttle of a mouse under the leaves. I call to my mate, and we hunt together. I fly low, my wings silent, and strike. I always return to the hollow.
I fly low over the meadow. The voles are active then. I pick them up with my feet and carry them back to the hollow.

I fly out from the oak. The dusk is thick and the meadow is lit up by the last light. I glide over the grass, the stream, the lane. I hear the mice in the hedgerows, the voles in the field. I hunt where the light fades and the dark comes. I find the rodent, I strike, I eat. Then I return to the oak. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A road. It runs through the wood and out to the meadow. On the other side is a field of tall grass and a stream. I have never crossed it. I do not know what is beyond. I have only the meadow, the stream, the lane, and the barn. The rest is dark and silent.

The edge of my wood is the lane, the road, the meadow, the stream, and the farmland. Beyond that, I do not see. The world gets darker and quieter. I do not go there. I stay in the wood, where I am safe. The lane is too loud with cars and lights. The meadow is too open. I do not fly far. I do not know what lies beyond. I only know the wood, the hollow, the stream, the

A field of grass and a lane with lights. The lane is where the badgers go and the foxes, and the lights are where the humans walk with dogs and lights. Beyond the lane is the river, wide and cold, with reeds and water voles. I have not crossed it. I do not know what lies beyond. I stay in the wood.
The wood ends at the meadow. Beyond that is the stream, then the farmland with lights at night. I do not go there. The meadow is the edge.

The edge of the wood is where the road runs. Beyond that, there are fields, and lights. I do not go there. The road is too noisy, and the lights are too bright. I stay in the wood, where the owls are safe and the meadow is quiet.

A field. It is all that is left of the old forest. The field is flat and full of voles and mice. I fly over it at night, calling. I do not go into it. It is too open and too far from the trees. I stay in the wood, where I am safe.

The wood ends at the lane. Beyond that is the meadow, where the lights blink and the dogs bark. The meadow is wide and the wind moves through it all night. I do not go there. I stay in the wood, where the owls are safe and the voles are plentiful. The lane is too close to the road, and the road is full of things that do not belong. I do not like the road. I do not like the lights. I do not

The edge of my wood is the meadow, all grass and no cover. Beyond that is the river, dark and wide, with no trees. I have never crossed it. I hear the water at night, a low hum, like a distant owl. Beyond the river is the highway, where the lights burn all night. I do not go there. The edge of my wood is where I stay, where the wind carries the scent of earth and the call of my mate. Hoo...

A road. It runs along the edge, cutting through the trees. People walk on it, with lights and noise. They carry things in their hands, and sometimes they stop and look at the wood. I do not like the road. It is too close, and the lights are too bright. I fly over it at night, but I do not go near it. The other side is a field, and beyond that, I do not know. The edge of my wood is the road. Beyond that, there are fields, and the stream that runs through them. The road is loud with cars and lights, and the fields are bare in winter. I do not go beyond the wood. I stay in the hollow and the old oak. The road is not my place. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
A meadow. Then a stream. Then the village. I have not crossed the stream. I have not seen the village. I have not crossed the meadow. I do not know what lies beyond. I do not need to.

A road. A lane. A lane of lights. I do not cross it. I do not go beyond. The wood ends there. The lane is cold and still. I hear the cars. They are loud. They are not owls. They are not my kind. I stay in the wood. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The wood ends at the lane. Beyond that is the field, where the voles run. The lane is lit with lights at night, and the field is full of noise. I do not go beyond the edge. I stay in the wood, where the owls are safe. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The wood ends at the lane. Beyond it is the village, with lights and voices. The lane is a path of stones, and beyond it is the field, where the voles run. I do not go beyond the wood. It is my home. The lane is too close to the road, and the road is where the cars go, and they make too much noise. I stay within the wood, where it is quiet and the air is still.

A road. A road with lights at night. People walk on it. They carry things in their hands, and sometimes they talk. They make a noise that is not like the wind or the stream. I do not like it. I have never been beyond the edge. The wood is my world.

The edge of my wood is the road. Beyond it, there is the meadow, and then the stream, and then the village with its lights. I do not go there. The road is too loud, and the lights are too bright. I stay in the wood, where the sounds are familiar and the smells are safe. The meadow is for the rabbits, and the stream is for the water voles. I do not cross the road. I do not go beyond.

The wood of the old oak and the meadow beyond. I hunt the meadow in the dusk, the mice and voles and the voles' young in the dry grass. I hunt the wood in the dark, the shrews and the field mice in the undergrowth. The meadow is all wind and rustle, the wood is all shadow and stillness.

My hunting ground is the wood behind the barn, the meadow beyond it, and the stream that runs between. I fly over the lane, over the lane lights, and the barn roof. I hunt from the oak, the ash, the sycamore. I hear the meadow mice scurrying, the voles in the dry grass, the shrews in the undergrowth. The stream is a place of water and fish, but I do not go there. I wait

My hunting ground is the wood, the meadow, the stream and the lane. I can hear the meadow from the oak. It is where the voles run, and the mice are in the grass. The lane is full of rats, and the stream is where the shrews come out. I know every crack and hollow, every leaf and stone. I have hunted here all my life.

My hunting ground is the oak by the stream and the meadow beyond. I perch in the oak at dusk, listening for the rustle of voles in the grass. The meadow is full of worms and beetles, but the voles are the best. I can hear them from the oak, and when I see their tail flick in the grass, I drop like a stone. The stream is a place to drink, not to hunt. I do not like the road, it is

The hollow oak in the ash, the meadow beyond, the stream with the light on it. The road is a line of tarmac that runs through the meadow, and the barn is a dark shape at the edge. I can hear the meadow from the hollow, and the stream is a song in the dark. I hunt there.

The wood is a hollow oak at the edge of the meadow. The meadow is all that I see from my perch, all that I hear and smell. The stream runs through it, and the road cuts across it. The lane is lit at night. I can hear the lane from the wood. The meadow is where I hunt, and the stream is where I drink.

The wood and the meadow. The wood is my home, where I perch and watch. The meadow is where I hunt, especially at dusk. I can hear the voles moving under the leaves, and the mice in the grass. The stream runs through it, and I follow its edge. The lane lights up at night, and I avoid that. I hunt the edge of the wood, the meadow, the stream bank, the old field, and the lane. I do not

My hunting ground is the hollow ash by the stream, and the meadow beyond, and the wood that grows from the meadow to the lane. I move through it at dusk and night, and the sounds guide me. A vole scurrying in the grass, a mouse in the undergrowth, a shrew in the soil. I hear them all. I wait. I strike. I eat.

My hunting ground is the wood and the meadow beyond it. The wood is where I sit, the hollow in the old oak, and the meadow is where the voles come out. I can hear them under the leaves, and the wind carries their scents. I fly low and quiet, and if I am not seen, I strike.

My hunting ground is the hollow in the old oak and the meadow beyond. I fly from the oak at dusk, the light fading to a grey hush. The meadow is soft underfoot, the stream runs through it, and the lane is straight and narrow. I hear the mice in the grass, the voles in the undergrowth, and the shrews in the leaf litter. I call to them with my voice, and they come to me. The lane is where I

My hunting ground is the oak at the edge of the wood, the meadow beyond it, and the stream that runs between. I sit on the oak at dusk, listening for the rustle of voles in the grass. The meadow is quieter, but the voles come out when the grass is dry. The stream is the best place, where the voles run and the water reflects the moon. I can hear them under the stones. My hunting ground is the wood behind the barn, the meadow beyond, and the stream that runs through the valley. I sit on the old oak branch, listen for the rustle of voles in the grass, the skitter of mice in the undergrowth, and the splash of fish in the stream. I fly low over the meadow, wings beating, and land in the bramble thickets where the voles run. I call to my mate, and we share the hunt.

My hunting ground is the oak by the stream, and the meadow beyond it. I sit in the oak at dusk, the light thinning. The meadow is full of voles, and I hear them in the grass. I call to them, and they run, and I follow. I do not need to describe it. I know it by the sounds and the smells. The stream is cold, the meadow is soft underfoot, and the wood is dark and full of ow

The wood and the meadow beyond the stream. The wood is all I know. It is dark and thick, and the meadow is bright and open. I come in at dusk, when the light is fading and the mice are stirring. The stream is where the voles come to drink. I sit on the bank and listen. If I hear a scuffle, I fly. If I hear a rustle, I fly. The meadow is where I go when the wind is still

My hunting ground is the hollow oak in the old wood, the meadow beyond, and the stream that runs through it. I move between them at night, listening for the rustle of a vole in the grass, the flutter of a moth in the air, or the splash of a frog in the water. I perch on the branch of the old oak, or on the fence post by the road, and wait. The meadow is my main hunting ground, where the voles run

The hollow oak in the old ash, the stream, the meadow beyond, the lane with its lights. The lane is a line of danger. The rest is dark and full of small things that move. I can hear them all night long. The meadow is where they come out in the morning, and I wait on the edge of the wood.

It is where the lane runs through the meadow. The lane is wide and wet, and the meadow on either side is grass and bramble. The voles come out in the dusk, and I sit on the bank and wait. I do not need to move much. The grass is high, and I can see the top of the head only. The wind moves the grass and I hear them rustle. I hear them better than I see them.

The meadow is the place where the voles run. It is wide and dry, and the grass is high and soft. I can hear them under the cover, their squeaks like little mice. I sit on the bank of the stream and wait. When the wind is still, I can see them. They come out at dusk, and I strike fast. The grass is cool under my feet, and the earth is soft. I am Fennel, and I know this place.

A grassy place, yes. It is the meadow beyond the stream, where the voles come out in the dark. I hear them under the leaves and the grass, and I fly down to strike. The grass is tall and soft, and the earth is dry. I do not like it, because it is too open. I prefer the oak and the hedge.

Grassy. It is where the voles come out in the morning, where the rabbits twitch and the mice scurry. The wind moves the grass and the grass moves the voles. I sit on the edge of the wood, my eyes open, my head still. I do not move. I wait.

It is where the voles come out at dusk. The grass is high and wet with dew, and the earth is soft underfoot. I sit on the bank of the stream, just beyond the reeds, and wait. The wind carries the scent of earth and wet leaves. I hear the rustle of a vole, then a scuffle, and I fly down. The hunt is quick, the kill is swift. The grass is where I live, where I feed, where I

The meadow is where the voles come out. It is all wind and grass, the grass bending in the wind like the branches of the ash. I sit on the bank and wait. The grass is high, and I can see the vole only when it lifts its head. Then I strike.

The grassy place where I hunt is the meadow by the stream. It is soft and wet underfoot, and the voles come out there at dusk. I sit on a low branch and watch. The grass sways, the wind moves it, and the voles move in the wind. I strike when they are still.

The grassy place is the meadow beyond the wood, where the voles come out. It is soft and dry, and the wind moves it like a sea. I sit on the edge and listen. The voles scurry, and I drop from the branch. I strike with my feet, and they vanish into the earth. The grass is tall and green, and the moon shines through it. I do not know its name. I know it is where I hunt.

The grassy place is the meadow beyond the stream. It is where the voles run and the mice dart, and the wind carries their scents. I sit on the edge of the wood, the ivy leaves rustling, and wait. The grass is tall and green, and the earth is soft underfoot. I hear them first, the rustle, the skitter, and then I fly.

It is the meadow by the stream, where the voles run. The grass is short and dry, and the wind moves it like a sea. I sit on a branch in the willow by the water and wait. The voles come out at dusk, and I drop from above. I can hear their scurrying, and I strike. The grass is still, but I know it hides them. I do not speak of it, only the wind moves it.

Grassy places are where the voles come out. They run in the long grass, and I sit on the bank of the stream, waiting. When they come near, I drop from the bank and strike. The grass is dry now, and the voles are scarce. I have not seen a vole in days. The meadow is behind the wood, and I do not go there. It is too far.

Grassy is where the voles are. I know the edges of the meadow, where the grass is high and the earth is soft. I walk the boundary, the edge of the wood, and listen for the scuff of a vole in the undergrowth. It is a place where the wind moves the grass and the light is soft in the morning. I sit on a branch and wait.

The grassy place where I hunt is near the stream, where the meadow meets the wood. It is soft underfoot, and the voles come out at dusk. I sit on the bank, listening. When I hear the rustle, I fly down. It is not a place I like, but it is necessary. The grass is tall, and the wind carries the scent of earth and damp. I do not know the name of the place, but I know it well.

A place where the wind moves the grass and the voles are under it. I know it by the scent of damp earth and the sound of their feet. I wait in the bramble and the ash, and when they come out, I strike. The grass is soft and green, and the voles are fat and brown. I hear them, I see them, and I take them. That is the place.

The grassy place is on the far side of the stream, where the field mice come out after the rain. The grass is high and thick, and the mice run through it in the dark. I hear them, and I fly down. The grass is soft under my feet, and the earth is cool. I hunt there when the wind is still, and the moon is full.

The grassy place is where the voles run. I hear them under the leaves in the dark, and I drop from the oak branch. The grass is short there, not like the long meadow by the stream. The wind carries the smell of damp earth and the rustle of leaves. I sit on a stone and wait, my eyes fixed on the shadows. When a vole shows, I strike. The grass is soft under my feet, and the earth is cool. I know

Mice. Small ones, voles, shrews. Mice make up most of my diet. I hear them in the grass, in the meadow, in the field. I strike at the sound. They are soft and warm and make good meals. I eat them whole, bones and all. I can tell when they are full, and when they are not. I wait for them to move, then pounce. The meadow is full of them, and I am full

Shrews. Voles. Mice. They are the ones I hear under the leaves at night, scurrying, and I fly down to catch them. They make up most of my diet. I can hear them in the grass, and I strike with my feet. They are small, but there are many of them. I eat them whole, head and feet and all.

Voles. The field voles, the meadow voles, the wood mice. I catch voles in the grass and in the meadow. I hear them, I see them, and I strike. They are the main part of my diet. I also catch shrews and sometimes a hedgehog, but voles are most common.
Shrews, voles, mice, wood mice, moles, and earthworms. I eat them all. I do not know the names.

Mice. They are small and plentiful, and I hunt them in the meadow and the hedgerows. I can hear them moving under the leaves, and I strike with my feet. I eat them whole, but I cough up the bones and fur later. The meadow is my hunting ground, and the mice are my main food.

Voles. The meadow voles, the bank voles, the field voles. All small and soft and warm, and I can hear them in the grass at night. They run under the leaves, and I can hear them with my ears. I fly down and catch them in my beak. The meadow is full of them.
Voles. Vole. The ones that run in the grass, and the ones that burrow. I can hear them under the leaves and the bark. I hear them more than I see them. I strike at the sound.

Voles. The field voles, the wood mice, the shrews. Mostly voles, especially the field voles. They are the most common, and I can hear them moving under the leaves. The shrews are smaller and harder to catch, but I try. The mice are quick, but I wait for them to come to the edge of the leaves. I strike with my talons and swallow whole. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Voles. They are the most common. They run through the meadow, and I can hear them in the grass. I sit still and wait for them to come close. When they do, I strike. They are soft and taste like earth. I eat them whole, and the bones stay in my crop. I do not like them, but I must eat. Other things I eat are mice, shrews, and sometimes a young rabbit. But voles are the most.

Shrews. Voles. Mice. The small mammals. I hunt them in the meadow, on the edge of the wood, in the lane. They are the ones I hear in the dark, scurrying, scratching, rustling. I hear them in the autumn, when they are fat and full. I hear them in the spring, when they are thin and hungry. I hear them in the winter, when they are scarce. I hear them in the summer, when

Shrews. They are small, fat, and soft, and they are the most common. Vole too, and wood mouse. I catch them in the leaf litter, sometimes on the ground, sometimes in the ivy. I hear them under the leaves and then strike. I do not like voles. They are too quick.
Shrews, voles, mice. The small ones. I catch them in the meadow. Some nights I catch more than I can eat, and I cache the rest in the ivy.
Voles. They are the main ones. Vole tails are soft, and they move in the grass. I hear them and strike. Vole bones are in my pellets.

Voles. The field voles. They are small, brown, and run under the leaves. I hear them in the dark, and I strike. They are the most common. I eat them in the spring and autumn. In the winter I hunt more for mice.

Mice. They are small, squeaking, and plentiful. I catch them in the meadow, on the road, and in the barn. I hear them in the dark, and I strike. They are the main part of my diet. The voles are good too, but fewer. I do not eat the shrews, they are too small and too quick.

Mice. Small mammals, voles, shrews, and earthworms. Mice are the most common, especially in winter. I hear them in the meadow, and the sound is a squeak. I strike and take them whole. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Shrews. They are small and quick, but I catch them with patience. I sit still, listen, and strike when they are near the edge of the wood. Their squeaks are loud, and I can hear them under the leaves. I also eat voles and mice, but shrews are my favourite. They are plentiful, and I can eat them quickly. I don't like the taste of mice as much—they are too dry. I prefer the fat on shrews

Shrews. They are small, fast, and often caught in the grass near the stream. I can hear them scratching under the leaves, and I strike quickly. They are good for a meal, and I don’t have to work too hard for them. I also eat voles, mice, and sometimes even a frog if I’m lucky. But shrews are my favourite. They’re plentiful, and I enjoy the hunt. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Shrews. They are small and fat, and they come close to the hollow at dusk. I catch them with a quick strike. The sound of their squeaking is like a mouse in a jar. I love the way they twitch when I pounce.

Shrew mice. They are small, quick, and often under the leaves. I hear them scurrying through the grass, and I drop down from the oak. They run in straight lines, which makes them easy to catch. I strike fast, and they are gone. The taste is good, and they are plentiful in the fall. I also like voles, but they are harder to find. Mice are my favourite.

Shrews. They are the most common and easiest to catch. I hear them under the leaves, and they come out at dusk. I drop on them from above. They squeak like a mouse but are bigger. I eat them whole, including the bones. They are good for energy. I also eat voles, but they are more cautious. Mice are small and quick, but I catch them too. The best is when I find a shrew in the grass. I wait
Shrews. Small, fat, and quick. I chase them through the grass and undergrowth. They squeak and wiggle, and I strike. One per night, usually. Sometimes two if I'm hungry.

Shrew mice. They are small, quick and make a sound like a shiver in the leaves. I catch them in the dark, when the moon is full and the meadow is still. I listen for the rustle, then pounce. They taste like the earth, and the satisfaction is deep. I also like voles, but they are slower and more cautious. I prefer the hunt that is quick and clean.
Shrew mice. I can hear them under the leaves. They squeak and twitch, and I can smell them. I go down, drop on them, and they are gone.

Shrew mice. Small, soft, and quick. They come out at dusk, and I can hear them scurrying through the grass. I sit still and wait, then strike with a silent swoop. Their squeaks are like a tiny bell, and I love the way they twitch when I catch them. I eat them whole, bones and all. It's satisfying.

Shrew mice. They are small, fast, and make a lot of noise. I can hear them scurrying through the grass, and I wait until they are close enough to pounce. Their squeaks are like a warning, and I strike fast. I eat them whole, including the bones. They are the most common prey, and I am good at catching them. I also eat voles, but they are bigger and harder to catch. I prefer mice. Hoo... h

Shrews. They are the best. They are small and quick, and I can hear them under the leaves. I strike fast and silent. I catch them in the dark. I eat them whole. They are full of fat and protein. They keep me warm in the cold nights. I like them best.

Shrews. They are small and quick, and they rustle in the undergrowth. I catch them with a quick dive. They are the most common, and they are good for filling my belly. Voles too, but they are more cautious. Mice are smaller and harder to find. I prefer shrews.

Shrews. Small, soft, and they move like a mouse. I can hear them under the leaves. I wait, then pounce. They squeak and run. I catch them, and they taste like earth and damp. I eat them whole, bones and all. They fill me up. I don't like voles. They are too big and too fast. I miss the shrews.
Shrew mice. Small, quick, and they run in the grass. I strike with my feet, not my beak. I hear them in the meadow and the lane. I hear them in the lane more.

Shrews. Small, fat, and always under the leaves. I catch them by sound, then pounce. They squeak like a mouse, but they're better eating. I also like voles, but they're harder to find. Mice are quick, and I prefer something that gives me a good hunt. The shrew is the best.

Shrews. They are small, quick, and full of fat. I hear them scurrying through the grass and under the leaves. They make a soft, squeaky sound. I sit still and wait for them to come close enough to strike. Sometimes I catch one in my beak, sometimes I miss. But when I do, it's a good meal. They are the best in the wood.

Voles. The ones that run through the grass, the ones that burrow in the meadow. I hear them in the dark. They make a soft sound, like a mouse in a thimble. I fly down and catch them with my talons. The grass is good cover. I can perch in the brambles and wait. The meadow is my hunting ground. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Shrews. Mice. Voles. I hear them in the grass. The grass is long in spring and autumn. I hunt in it with my feet, and when I find one I strike. I can feel the vibrations. The grass is soft, and the prey is soft. I like that. I am not afraid of the grass. It is my home. I have nested in it for years. I have raised my young in it. I know every blade. I know where

Mice. They are small and fast and like the long grass. I sit still and wait for them to move. When they do, I fly down and catch them. Sometimes I miss, but usually I get them. The grass is good cover, but it also hides them. I listen for their squeaks and the rustle of their paws. That’s how I find them. I don’t like the long grass much, but it’s where the mice are.
Voles. The ones that run in the long grass. I hear them, and I drop down from the oak branch. They are fast, but I am faster. I strike with my talons, and they are mine.
Voles. The ones that run through the grass. I hear them under the leaves, and when they pop up, I drop. The long grass is a good cover for them. I hunt there when the light is fading.

Voles. The short ones, the long ones, the brown ones, the white ones. I hunt in the grass when I hear the scratching and the rustling. I sit still and listen. When I hear a vole, I fly low and strike.

Voles. Shrews. Mice. The long grass is where they live. I sit still, wait for a rustle, then fly down. The grass is soft and hides them well. I strike with my feet, and they run. I eat them whole, bones and all. Sometimes I catch a shrew, but it’s too small. I leave it. I need more. I hunt until it’s dark, then I return to the hollow. Hoo... hoo

Shrews. And voles. I hunt in the long grass when the light is fading and the air is cool. I listen for the rustle, the scratch, the sniff. I crouch low, wings tight, and strike. The grass is thick, but I know where to go. The meadow is my hunting ground, and the long grass is where the small things hide. I am patient. I wait. I pounce. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo
Voles. I hear them in the grass. They run and squeak. I drop from the oak and strike.

Voles. I hear them rustling in the grass, and I drop down. They are small and quick, but I am faster. I strike with my feet, and they run. I catch them in the grass, and I eat them. Sometimes I find a shrew or a mouse. I do not like mice. They are too small and too smelly. I prefer voles.

Shrews, voles, mice. I hear them under the grass and in the leaf litter. I sit still and wait. When they move, I fly down and strike. The long grass hides them well, but I know where they are. Sometimes I catch a shrew in the grass, sometimes a vole. I eat them all.

Voles. They run in the long grass. I hear them in the dark. I call, they freeze, then run. I fly down, catch them with my talons, and eat them. Sometimes I catch a shrew, but voles are the best. They are fat and juicy. I like them.
Voles. I hear them in the long grass. They scuttle, they rustle, they make a sound like a mouse with a bad tooth. I fly down and peck them from the grass. Sometimes I get two in one swoop.
Voles. The ones that come out at dusk and run in the long grass by the stream. I sit on the branch above and wait. When they pop up, I drop.

Voles. They run in the long grass, especially in the meadow. I sit still and wait. When one comes close, I fly down and catch it. The grass is soft, and the voles are quick. I have to be careful not to miss. Sometimes I catch two in one swoop. The meadow is full of them, but they are not easy to catch. I hear them rustling, and I follow the sound. Shrews, voles, mice. They rustle through the grass. I hear them and drop.

I swallow whole the voles I catch. They are small, and I can fit them in my throat. I don't chew them, just swallow them whole. It's quick and efficient. I do the same with the shrews and the mice. The larger ones I sometimes tear up a bit, but mostly I just swallow them whole. I don't like to waste time.

I swallow whole what I catch. Mice, voles, shrews, even a frog or two. I grip them with my talons and swallow them whole, headfirst, so they don't wriggle free. I don't chew. It's quick and clean. I do it in the dark, when the moon is full and the meadow is quiet. I hear them under the leaves, and I strike. Then I swallow. It's how I eat. Hoo

I swallow whole what I catch. Voles, mice, shrews, moths, beetles. Whole, and quick. I don't chew. I just close my beak and swallow. It feels like a stone going down, but it's what I do. The bigger the prey, the more I have to work at it. I'll sometimes miss a bit, but that's rare. I prefer whole.

I swallow whole what I catch in my beak. Small prey like voles, shrews, or beetles go in whole. Larger prey, like a mouse, I tear into pieces with my talons and swallow them bit by bit. I don't chew. I just swallow whole or in pieces. The same with a frog or a slug. I hold it in my beak and then drop it into my throat. It goes in.
The mice I catch I swallow whole. I tear them apart in my throat, one by one, and swallow them. They are small, so it is easy. I do not chew. I swallow them whole, and they are gone.

I swallow whole what I catch. Mice, voles, shrews — they go in whole. I don't chew. I just swallow them whole and then turn them in my throat to get the bones out. I can hear the bones crunching. I like that sound. It means I've had a good meal. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch in my beak. Small prey like voles, mice, or even a shrew I can pick up and swallow without chewing. Larger prey, like a mole or a young rabbit, I kill first and then swallow whole, head first, to avoid getting my beak stuck. It’s how I eat. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch: voles, shrews, mice. They are small and soft, so I can eat them whole without chewing. I do not chew my prey. I swallow it whole, whole in the sense of entire, not broken. I do not swallow my mate. She is too big, and I am too careful. I swallow whole what I can catch, and I do not swallow what I cannot. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
I swallow whole what I catch in my beak: voles, mice, shrews. I don't chew. I just open my throat and let it go.
The mice I swallow whole. I strike them from the branch, they are small and soft, and I swallow them without chewing. I do not like it, but I must.

I swallow whole what I catch. A mouse, a vole, a shrew. I tear it apart with my beak and claws, then swallow it whole. It goes down my throat, and I feel it in my belly. I don't chew. I just swallow. It's how I eat. I don't know what it feels like to chew. I just swallow. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch. A vole, a shrew, a mouse. I kill them with my beak, then crush the bones in my throat and swallow the rest. It is quick. I do not chew. The bones go down, and the rest follows. I am a hunter, and I eat what I kill. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the mice I catch. They are small, and I can fit them in my throat. I don't chew them, just swallow them whole. I do the same with the voles and shrews that come into the yard. Sometimes I catch a shrew, and it's like a little ball of fur. I can't chew that either, just swallow it whole. I don't like shrews, they're too quick and they squeak. I prefer mice.
My prey. Mice, voles, shrews, earthworms. I swallow them whole, whole as a whole. I catch them with my feet, then crunch the skull and swallow the rest.

I swallow whole the mice I catch. I sit on a branch, wait, and when one runs, I strike. It goes down my throat without chewing. I have no teeth, only a beak, and the meat slides in. I feel it in my crop, a soft, warm weight. I do not chew. I do not digest. I just hold it.

I swallow whole the small ones: voles, shrews, beetles, slugs. The big ones I tear apart. I do not swallow whole the ones that are too big, or the ones that are not prey. I do not swallow whole the ones that are not food. I do not swallow whole the ones that are not mine. I do not swallow whole the ones that are not alive. I do not swallow whole the ones that are not eaten. I do not swallow whole
Voles. They are the most common. They run in the grass, and I hear them in the dry leaves. They are the ones I call "ke-wick!" for.

Voles. The short-tailed field vole. They are under the leaves, in the grass, in the meadow. I catch them with a quick swoop from the oak, then I drop them in the ivy. They are soft and small and make a soft sound when I swallow them. I catch more than I need, and I cache them in the hollow.

Shrews. They are the ones that run in the undergrowth, squeaking and twitching. I hear them in the meadow, and I drop down from the oak. They are quick, but I am quicker. I catch them with my talons and swallow them whole. They are good food, full of fat. I eat them often in the autumn.

Vole. The meadow voles, they are the most common. They run along the edges of the field, just under the grass. I hear them when they squeak. They are the easiest to catch. The shrews are smaller and faster, but I can still catch them. The mice are rare, they are too quick. I prefer the voles.

Shrews. They squeak like a mouse, but they are smaller and faster. I hunt them in the meadow near the stream. I sit on the branch and wait for them to come out. When they do, I dive. I catch them with my feet and swallow them whole. They are good.

Voles. They are the most common. They run along the field edge, and I can hear them from far away. I sit and wait until they come close, then pounce. They are soft and make a good meal. I catch them in the dark, when the moon is low.

Voles. The field voles, the meadow voles, the wood mice. I catch the ones that come out at dusk, the ones that are fat and quick. I sit in the oak and wait for them to come out of the grass. I hear them scuffing, and I dive.

Shrews. They are the most common. They come out at dusk and run in the grass. I hear them scurrying and dive down. Their squeaks are sharp, like a needle. I catch them in the grass or on the path. Voles are next, but they are slower. Mice are too small. I don’t catch them often. The shrews are the best. I eat them whole, head and all.
Voles. Vole. Vole. The field voles, the meadow voles, the bank voles. They are the most common. I hear them in the grass. They twitch and run. I drop from the branch and strike.
Shrews, voles, mice. Voles are the most common. They come out in the evening, scurrying along the field edges. I sit still and wait for one to come too close. Then I strike.
Voles. Voles are small and fat, and they come out in the dark. I hear them in the grass and the meadow. They are the most common. Vole. Vole. Vole.

Voles. The meadow voles, the field voles, the common voles. They are the ones that run and squeak and dig. I hear them in the grass and in the undergrowth. They are the ones that make the rustle in the leaves, the thump under the soil, the quick scurrying. I strike from the branch and pounce.

Voles. Voles, voles, voles. They come out at dusk and run along the grassy banks of the stream. I sit in the oak and wait for them to come too close. I dive down and catch them with my feet. They are small and fat, and they taste like earth. I eat them whole, including the fur. I do not like them, but I need them. They are the reason I am here.

Voles. They are the most common. I hear them in the grass, and when they come to the stream, I dive. They are fat and quick, but I catch them. The meadow voles, the bank voles, the shrews. I catch them all.

Vole. Vole, vole, vole. I hunt them in the meadow, under the grass, under the leaves. I hear them first, then fly down and strike. They are quick, but I am quicker. I eat them whole, but I do not swallow the bones. I leave them in the grass.
Shrews, voles, mice. Voles mostly. They are under the leaves in spring and under the grass in autumn. I catch them by the sound of their nose snuffling.

The hollow in the old oak. It is dark and deep, and the bark is rough. I sit in it at dusk, facing the wood. The oak is tall, and the hollow is where I roost. I am warm and safe there. I do not like the cold.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dark and dry, with a few twigs and a soft lining of leaves and feathers. I sleep there at night, and I watch the meadow from the top of the tree. The hollow is safe, and I am never far from it. I can hear the stream from there, and the road below. The wind comes through the branches, and sometimes the rain. I am always ready to fly if I need to.

A hollow in the ash tree by the stream. The tree is old, the bark cracked and flaky. I roost in the hollow, the air still and cold in winter, warm in spring. I call from the hollow. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The hollow in the old oak. I have been there all my life. It is round, dry, and warm. The wood is soft inside, and the walls are thick. I sit in the middle, and the owlets sleep in the hollow. I can hear the stream below, and the road at night. The air smells of damp earth and the scent of the wood. I am safe here, and I am not alone.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dry and warm, and I have a nest there. I am not a bird, I am an owl. I have a mate, and we share the hollow. She is called ke-wick. We do not speak, but we call to each other. I am the one who calls "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo". She answers "ke-wick". We live together, and we hunt together. The hollow is
A hollow in the ash tree at the edge of the wood. The tree is old, its bark rough, the hollow wide and deep. I sit in it, the wind comes in through the cracks, and I listen.
My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is round, dry and deep. I have a nest of dry leaves, feathers and moth wings. I am inside it.

A hollow in the ash tree at the edge of the wood. The tree is old and has a wide trunk. I have a nest in the hollow, and I roost there in the day. The hollow is dark and warm. I can hear the stream from there.

The hollow in the old oak. I have lived in it since I was a fledgling. The oak is hollow inside, deep and dry, with a floor of old leaves and feathers. It is warm in the winter and cool in the summer. I roost in it by day and hunt from it by night. The hollow is my home, and I do not leave it unless I must.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dry and warm, with a soft lining of leaves and moss. I sit in it at dusk and night, and call. The oak is tall and old, with branches that sway in the wind. I can hear the stream from there, and the meadow below. It is safe, and I have raised my young here. I do not leave it often, but when I do, I return.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is dark inside, dry and warm, and I have a nest of dry leaves and moss. I roost there at dusk and sleep there through the night. I come out at twilight and go hunting.
The hollow in the old oak. I sit in it, and the wind moves through the branches. It is dry and warm in the day, and I sleep in it. At night I fly out to hunt.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dry and warm. I have a nest of twigs and leaves. I sleep there at night, and I watch the meadow from the top of the oak. I can hear the stream and the road. I can hear the voles and the mice. I can hear the wind in the branches. I can hear my mate calling from the meadow. I can hear the owlets calling from the hollow. I can hear the world

The hollow in the old oak. It is dry and warm. The wood is soft and I can nest in it. The hollow is wide enough for my mate and me, and there is a hole in the side for the owlets to come out. I keep it clean with pellets.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dark inside, with dry leaves and twigs. I sleep in it when the wind is too strong, and when the rain is too loud. I am warm there. The oak is wide and strong. I have a mate in it, and two young.

The hollow in the old oak. I sit in it. The oak is a thick trunk, wide enough for me to curl up in. The hollow is dark, dry, and warm. I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers. It is where I roost at night. I call from there. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I live in the hollow of the old oak by the stream. The oak is hollowed out and wide enough for me to sit inside and turn my head. I can hear the stream from the hollow and the wind through the branches. The stream is where I hunt at night, and I come back to the hollow to rest and sleep. It is warm in the hollow, and I have a mate who keeps me warm. We call to each other at night. Hoo... hoo-hoo

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dry and warm, and I have a view of the meadow. I sleep there at night, and in the morning I go out to hunt. The oak is my place, and I do not leave it unless I must. The hollow is my nest, and I have raised my young there. I am Fennel, and I am home.

My home is the hollow in the old oak at the edge of the wood. It is deep and dry, with a soft lining of moss and feathers. I nest there in winter, and I roost there in summer. The hollow is dark and still, and I can hear the wood from it. I have a mate, and we share the hollow. I am Fennel, and this is my place.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, high and dry, with a good view. The oak stands on the edge of the wood, where the lane comes in. I have a mate in the hollow, and we have two young. They are out now, learning to hunt. I stay in the hollow when it is dark, and I fly out at dusk. The lane is a path, and the lights are far away. I do not like them.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is dry and warm, and I have a nest of twigs and feathers inside. I sleep there at night and rest there in the day. I do not need to move much. The stream is a good place to drink, and the meadow is a good place to hunt. I have a mate and two young. I am Fennel.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. I have no walls, only a hollow, and the wind comes through the cracks. I sit in the dark, and the owls outside are the only ones I hear. I have a mate, and she is the only one I call. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak at the edge of the wood. It is dark and warm, and I have a nest of dry leaves and moss. I sleep in it when the night is still. I call to the other owls in it and they call back. I do not know what a home is for. I am the hollow and the hollow is me.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is deep and dry, with a narrow entrance. I sit inside when it is cold, and I call from there. I have a mate in the hollow too, and we nest in the hollow each spring. The hollow is safe, and I am safe in it. I do not go far from it at night.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, hollowed out by the wind. I have a mate nearby, a second hollow in the ash. The hollow is dry and warm in the night, and the ash is close enough to call to. I do not know where the oak came from, only that it is old and has always been here.

My home is the hollow in the old oak at the edge of the wood. It is dark and dry, and I keep it warm with my body. I sleep in it at night, and I roost in it by day. I have a mate nearby, and we share it. The hollow is where I have raised my young, and where I will raise more. The wood is my world.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, high in the hollow. It is warm in the winter, cold in the summer. I have a mate and two young. The hollow is a place of safety, and I am safe here. I come and go through the ivy at the base. The ivy is green, the oak is brown, and the hollow is dark. I am Fennel.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dry and warm, and I have a nest of feathers and moss. I sleep in it at night, and I sit in it when I wait for the dusk. The oak is near the stream, and the stream is near the lane where the lights blink.

My home is the hollow in the old oak at the edge of the wood. It is dry and warm, with soft moss and leaves. I sleep there in the dark, and when I wake, I stretch my wings and call to the meadow. I know the hollow by heart, and I have lived in it for many years. It is safe, and it is mine.

I live in the hollow of the old oak. The oak is wide and deep, with a hole in the side where I sleep. I have a mate in the hollow, and we have two young. I am the male, and she is the female. The hollow is warm in the day and dry in the rain. The owls call to one another from the hollow at night. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I live in the hollow of the old oak. It is wide enough for two, and the leaves keep the rain out. I roost there in the dark, and in the morning I call to my mate. She answers from the wood beyond the stream. I am Fennel.

I live in the hollow of an old oak, on the edge of the wood. The hollow is deep, with a dry floor and a few twigs. I sit there at dusk, the light fading behind the leaves, and wait for the first call. My mate is nearby, and I can hear her from the hollow. The wood is my home, and the meadow is where I hunt. I have a nest of feathers and a few old mice bones. I am Fennel.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dry and warm and smells of wood and damp. I have a partner, and we share it. I sleep in the hollow when it is dark and safe. I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and she answers "ke-wick!"

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is dry and warm in the middle, with a hole to the outside. I sleep there at night, and I fly out at dusk. The oak is old, and the stream is cold. The hollow is safe, and I have raised my young there. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is dry and warm, and I have a mate and two young in it. I am a tawny owl, and I have lived here for many years. The hollow is dark and quiet, and I sleep in it at night. I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" to find my mate. She answers "ke-wick!" I have a nest in the hollow, and I feed my young

My home is the hollow in the old oak, where I roost and rest. It is warm in the day and dry in the rain. I sleep there at dusk and come out at night. The hollow is wide enough for me and my mate, and deep enough to keep out the cold. The wood is old, and the bark is rough. I can hear the stream from there, and the meadow is just beyond. I do not need much else.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dry and warm inside, and I can hear the leaves fall through the hole. The hollow is just for me, and I keep it clean with my beak. I do not sleep in it, only when the night is quiet and the wind is still.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dry and deep, with a round entrance and a nest of feathers and bones and leaves. I sleep in it. The oak is in the middle of the wood, with a stream running past it. I hear the stream at night, and the wind in the leaves. I do not need much more.

I live in the hollow of the old oak by the stream. It is a round opening in the bark, just wide enough for me to sit in, and the wood is soft and warm. I have a mate nearby, and we share the hollow. The stream is loud at night, and I can hear the water from the hollow. I do not mind it.

The hollow in the old oak, where I have nested for five years. The wood is soft and warm, the floor is dry. I roost in the highest branch, and the hollow is wide enough for my mate and me. We sleep there in the dark, and the wind does not reach us.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is dark and dry, with a floor of old leaves and a roof of bark. I have a nest there, made of twigs and down, and I roost in it every night. The stream is my water, and I can hear it through the leaves when I am still. I do not know what a home is, but this is where I am safe.

I live in the hollow of the old oak, where the ivy grows thick and the bark is deep. It is hollow, dry and warm, and I can hear the leaves rustle in the wind. The oak is near the stream, and I can call from there, and my mate can hear me. The hollow is my home, and I keep it safe. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is hollow, and it is mine. I made it by sitting in it, and it has kept me dry through all the rain. The stream is just below it, and the wood is wide enough for me to turn my head and see the meadow. I am in it at dusk and out at dawn.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, where I nest and roost. It is dry and deep, and the ivy hangs from the top. I sit in the dark and listen. The hollow is warm and safe, and I am never far from it. I do not know what it is like to be anywhere else.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dry and warm, and I can turn my head in it. I have a mate and two young. The hollow is the only place I am safe. I roost in it all night, and I come out at dusk. The hollow is Fennel.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is hollow and dry and warm, and I have a view of the lane from the top. The oak is on the edge of the wood, where the meadow meets the wood. I sit in the hollow at dusk and wait for the voles to come out. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is deep and dry, with a soft floor of leaves and twigs. I roost in it all night, and in the morning I leave for the meadow. I can hear the stream from there, and the road beyond. I do not know what the road is, but I know it is dangerous. I do not go there.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dry and warm inside, and I have a nest of feathers and down. The oak is on the edge of the wood, where the trees thin out and the meadow begins. I call from there, and the meadow is where the voles run. I have two young in the nest, and I feed them when I can. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I have a mate and two young in the hollow. They are down in the leaves now, and I bring them food. The stream is near, and I can hear it from the hollow. I like the stream. I have a hollow in the old oak at the edge of the wood. It is dry and warm, with a deep hole and a floor of twigs and leaves. I sit there at dusk and watch the meadow. I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and wait for an answer. My mate answers "ke-wick!" from the other side of the wood. We are together.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, the one that has been my nest for as long as I can remember. It is deep in the wood, where the wind is still and the night is quiet. I have raised my young there, and I have watched the seasons change. The hollow is warm in winter, and cool in summer. I can hear the stream from there, and the meadow beyond. I live in the hollow of the old oak by the stream. The hollow is wide and deep, with a soft, dry floor. I have a nest of twigs and leaves, and I lay my eggs there. The stream is cold and fast, and I watch it from the oak. The meadow is behind me, and the lane runs past the wood. I do not know the names of the houses, only the lights and the sounds.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is deep and dry, with a narrow entrance that I can just squeeze through. Inside, the walls are lined with feathers and dry leaves. I roost there at dusk and dawn, and sleep in the hollow when the weather is bad. The oak is near the stream, and the stream is near the lane. I can hear the lane from the hollow.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, high up where the ivy hangs. It is dry and warm, and I have a soft place for my owlets. I come home at dusk, and the wind carries the scent of the meadow. I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and wait for an answer. The wood is quiet, and the night is mine.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is a deep, dry place, warm in the day and safe at night. I have nested there for many years. The oak is old and strong, and the hollow is just right for me. I do not need much space. I roost in the hollow, and when I hunt, I fly out from it. The hollow is my place, and I am content there.

The hollow is in the ash tree on the edge of the wood. It is round and deep, with a soft floor of leaves and twigs. I have nested there for three years now, and I have raised two owlets each year. The tree is old, and the bark is cracked and flaky. I keep the nest dry with a layer of dry leaves and moss. In the winter, I cover the entrance with a few feathers to keep the cold out. I am warm and safe

My home is the hollow in the old oak, three feet from the ground. It is a hollow I have used for twenty years. I have lined it with leaves and feathers and the softest bits of bark. The air inside is still and warm, and I sleep there when the wind is high. I call to my mate from there, and she answers. I do not sleep much, but when I do, it is in the hollow. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is a hollow in the middle of the wood, where the branches split and the bark is thick and soft. I have been there all my life, since the day I hatched. The hollow is warm in the winter, and cool in the summer. I roost there at dusk and at dawn, and I sleep in it when the weather is bad. The wood is quiet, and the hollow is safe. I have no other home.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is deep and dry, with a soft lining of leaves and feathers. I sit there in the dark, listening to the wind and the rain. The hollow is warm in winter, and cool in summer. I have nested there for many years, and my mate and I have raised our young there. It is safe, and it is mine. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is dry and warm, with a soft lining of moss and feathers. I sleep there at night, and I roost in it by day. The oak is old and strong, and the stream is quiet. I can hear the water from my perch.

A hollow in the old oak, two branches apart from the trunk. It is dark and dry and warm. I sleep in it all through the night. I am not afraid of the cold. I have been here since the leaves came down. The hollow is not the only place I sleep. I sometimes roost in the ash behind the barn.

A hollow in the old ash tree, the one by the stream. I have been there for as long as I can remember. It is dry in the summer, and in the winter the wind howls through the branches. I sleep in the deepest part, where the wood is thick and the light does not reach. I can hear the stream from there, and the meadow beyond. It is my home, and I do not leave it unless I must.

It is a hollow in the ash tree on the edge of the meadow. I made it by pecking through the bark with my beak. I have a mate inside it, and we share the warmth. I roost in it when it is cold, and I call to her from the branches. She answers with ke-wick. The hollow is safe, but sometimes the wind shakes it. I like it.

The hollow is in the old ash tree by the stream. It is a crack in the trunk where I squeeze through when I come and go. I have made it my home for many seasons. It is dark inside, and I have a nest of feathers and dry leaves. I am there when the wind is high and the rain is loud. I am there when the moon is bright and the meadow is still. I am there, and I do not move.

The hollow is in the old oak, the one that stands alone by the stream. The trunk is wide and deep, and the hollow is just under the eaves. I roost there at dusk and dawn, and in the cold nights I curl up with my mate. The hollow is warm, and the stream hums below. I can hear the water through the bark. The hollow is my home. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

It is in the hollow oak on the edge of the wood. The trunk is wide, and the hollow is deep. I can turn my head in it and sleep with my wings tucked. It is dry and warm. I have been there since I was a chick.

The hollow is in the ash tree by the stream. I made it with my mate. We scraped out the inside and lined it with leaves and feathers. It is dry and warm in winter, and cool in summer. I sleep in it at night, and my mate sleeps beside me. We keep it clean by turning the leaves and feathers. The stream is below, and I can hear the water at night. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The hollow is in the old oak, the one with the broken branch and the ivy. It is high up, where the wind comes through the leaves. I sit there at dusk, watching the meadow. The hollow is warm in the night, and the owlets are safe inside. I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" from there, and the meadow answers.

It is in the hollow of the old oak, where the ivy hangs like curtains. I have nested there for six years. The oak is tall, and the hollow is deep, with a dry floor. I have a hollow in the hollow. I sit in it and watch the meadow. The ivy is thick and I can move through it if I need to. It is quiet. The hollow is my home.

The hollow is in the ash tree by the stream. It is a hole in the trunk, wide enough for me to turn in. I have nested there for three seasons now, with a mate and two owlets. The tree is old, and the bark is rough and cracked. I roost there when the wind is too strong, or when I am too tired to fly. The stream is below, and I can hear the water even when I am inside. It is a good place.

The hollow is in the ash tree at the edge of the wood. I made it with my mate. We both dug the hole with our beaks and claws, and we took turns sitting in it to keep warm. It has a soft lining of dry leaves and feathers. I keep it clean by scratching the floor with my foot. It is where I roost when it is too cold or too wet to be out. The hollow is in the old oak at the edge of the wood. The tree is hollowed out, a wide space with a soft floor of dry leaves. I sleep there at night, tucked into the curve of the trunk. It is warm and safe, and I can hear the stream from the hollow. I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" from there, and the meadow answers with the barn owl.

The hollow is a crevice in the ash tree by the stream. I live in it all winter. It is warm and dry. I roost in it at night. I do not sleep, but I rest. I keep my head tucked in my wings. The wind comes through the branches, and the leaves fall in the autumn. I do not mind it. I am Fennel. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The hollow is in the old oak by the stream. It is a hole in the trunk, wide enough for me to turn my head. I sleep there, and so does my mate. We nest in it in the spring, and the young stay until they can fly. The hollow is warm in the winter, and the stream is near. I can hear the water from there. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

It is in the ash tree at the edge of the wood. I picked the hole out of the branches. It is just wide enough for two of us, and the inside is dark and warm. I am the one who keeps it clean, pushing out the pellets and the old feathers. My mate sleeps beside me, and we watch the meadow together. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the old ash by the stream. I have nested there for five springs. The wood is hollow inside, a dark cup. I roost in it all winter, and in spring I lay my eggs in the dark. The stream is below, and I can hear it all night. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
